passage: Zubin sat on the charpai watching cartoons on his uncle's phone, very still. Lokesh took the phone away gently and lifted him to the cowshed. "Look, the calf! What does it say?" Zubin stared, then shouted "Maa!" He patted the calf and laughed. Later, Lokesh sang the calf song and Zubin clapped along, trying the words.

qa.q: What was Zubin watching on his uncle's phone?
qa.a: He was watching cartoons.

qa.q: What does Zubin patting the calf and laughing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was delighted and far more lively with the real calf and Lokesh than with the cartoon.

qa.q: How did Lokesh help Zubin learn more?
qa.a: Lokesh showed him a real calf, asked questions and sang with him, giving live interaction.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel seeing Zubin try the words?
qa.a: Lokesh might feel happy and sure that playing together is good for him.

grounding: It shows a toddler learning better through live interaction than through a screen alone.

passage: In Buenos Aires, Diego sat with Tomas on the sofa to video-call Abuela. "Who's that?" Diego asked. Tomas pointed at the screen. "Buela!" Abuela held up a toy dog and barked. Tomas giggled and barked back. When the call ended, Diego switched off the tablet and handed Tomas his own toy dog. They crawled around the rug barking together.

qa.q: Who did Diego and Tomas video-call?
qa.a: They video-called Abuela.

qa.q: What does Tomas barking back suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he was delighted and joining in the game with Abuela.

qa.q: What did Diego do that made screen time better for Tomas?
qa.a: Diego sat with him, asked questions, then turned off the tablet and played with him live.

qa.q: How might Abuela feel about the call?
qa.a: She would probably feel close to her grandson and happy he responded to her.

grounding: It shows co-viewed screen exposure followed by live play for a toddler.

passage: I'm Joseph, and my little neighbour Tenzin is almost two. Some mornings he sits alone with a tablet, watching colourful animations, and when I say hi he doesn't look up. But when his grandmother reads him a picture book, he points, names things, and laughs. Yesterday she asked him "Where's the duck?" and he found it, then showed me. I don't know exactly why, but he seems much more alive with her.

qa.q: What does Tenzin watch alone on some mornings?
qa.a: He watches colourful animations on a tablet.

qa.q: What does Tenzin finding the duck and showing Joseph suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels engaged and proud when he learns with his grandmother.

qa.q: How could Tenzin's family use this?
qa.a: They could spend more time reading and talking with him, and watch screens together when used.

qa.q: How does Joseph see the difference in Tenzin?
qa.a: Joseph thinks Tenzin seems much more alive with his grandmother than with the tablet.

grounding: A neighbour observes that a toddler learns better with live interaction than with screens alone.

passage:
Monday: A cartoon played on the tablet while Mahima cooked. Vijay, two, stared at it, silent, not smiling.

Wednesday: Mahima sat with him and a picture book instead. "Cow! What does a cow say?" Vijay pointed. "Moo!" He turned pages, giggling.

The next weekend: They watched a short video of elephants together. Mahima paused it. "Big ear! Where's your ear?" Vijay grabbed his ear, then trumpeted like an elephant, laughing.

qa.q: What did Mahima and Vijay look at together on Wednesday?
qa.a: They looked at a picture book together.

qa.q: How did Vijay's mood differ between Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday he stared silently without smiling, while on Wednesday he giggled and joined in, suggesting he enjoyed being with Mahima.

qa.q: What worked about how Mahima used the elephant video?
qa.a: Mahima watched it with him, paused and asked questions, turning the screen into a shared, talking moment.

qa.q: What would change if Vijay only watched cartoons alone?
qa.a: He would miss the back-and-forth talk and play that helped him say words and laugh with Mahima.

grounding: Shows over several days how a toddler learns more through live interaction and shared viewing than a screen alone.

passage:
On Sunday morning in their Lucknow flat, Nitin found a short video of ducks for Ayesha, twenty-two months. He sat her on his lap.

"Duck! Quack quack!" he said. Ayesha flapped her arms. "Quack!"

When it ended she whined for more. Nitin shut the phone. "Let's find a real duck."

They walked to the park pond. When a real duck paddled past, Ayesha squealed and pointed, then looked at him.

"Yes! Duck," he said. She waddled after it, quacking.

qa.q: Where did Nitin and Ayesha go after the video?
qa.a: They walked to the park pond to find a real duck.

qa.q: What did Ayesha feel when the video ended, and later at the pond?
qa.a: She was unhappy when it ended and whined for more, but at the pond she was thrilled, squealing and pointing.

qa.q: Which of Nitin's choices helped Ayesha most?
qa.a: Watching together briefly and then taking her to see a real duck turned a short screen moment into live, shared learning.

qa.q: What is it like for Nitin when Ayesha whines for more video?
qa.a: It may be tempting to give in, but he chose a better alternative, and her joy at the pond likely made it worth it.

grounding: Shows a parent keeping screen time short and co-viewed, then moving to live interaction.

passage:
“Ritu won't eat,” said Nitin's wife, holding the spoon. “Give her your phone. The rhyme video works.”
Nitin looked at Ritu, eighteen months old, pushing the bowl away.
“Wait. Let me try.” He sat opposite her. “Machli jal ki rani hai!” He wiggled his hand like a fish.
Ritu stared. Then she wiggled her hand too.
“Jeevan uska paani hai!”
Ritu laughed and opened her mouth for the spoon.

qa.q: What did Nitin wiggle like a fish?
qa.a: He wiggled his hand like a fish.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when her father sang the rhyme?
qa.a: She was delighted and engaged, laughing and copying his hand.

qa.q: Why was singing live better than handing over the phone?
qa.a: Nitin could watch and respond to Ritu, so she joined in and learned instead of just watching.

qa.q: How might Nitin's wife see the live rhyme?
qa.a: She may be pleasantly surprised that it worked as well as the video.

grounding: A father chooses a live rhyme over a phone video to engage his toddler at mealtime.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday. Teacher: Maria.
Kishore's parents asked if cartoons would help his words. Today I read our duck picture book with him on my lap. I pointed and said “duck” and quacked. He watched my mouth, then pointed and said “Duh!” Three times.
After last week's cartoons, no new words.
Next step: I told his parents a short cartoon is fine if they watch with him and talk about it 😊

qa.q: What book did Maria read with Kishore?
qa.a: Maria read their duck picture book.

qa.q: How did Kishore seem to feel during the picture-book reading?
qa.a: He seemed curious and engaged, watching her mouth and trying the word.

qa.q: What was sensible about Maria's advice to Kishore's parents?
qa.a: Maria didn't forbid cartoons, but suggested watching with him and talking, because he learns best from live interaction.

qa.q: What is it like for Kishore's parents to receive this note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured and have a clear, gentle idea of how to help his words.

grounding: A daycare teacher notes a toddler learning words from live reading more than from cartoons.

passage:
During Navroz in Udvada, Tanuja's cousin called from abroad on a video call. Two-year-old Zubin stared at the little face on the phone.
Tanuja sat him on her lap and pointed. “See, Rustom Mama! Say hello!”
Zubin waved. Rustom waved back. Zubin laughed.
After two minutes, Zubin wriggled down and ran to the courtyard, where Dada was feeding the hens. He threw grain and shouted, “Chicken! Chicken!”

qa.q: Who did Zubin see on the phone?
qa.a: He saw Rustom Mama on the video call.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when Rustom waved back?
qa.a: He was surprised and happy, laughing at the wave.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do well during the call?
qa.a: She held Zubin on her lap and named and pointed at things, so he wasn't watching alone.

qa.q: How might Rustom feel during the short call?
qa.a: He may feel happy to see Zubin, even if the toddler soon ran off to play.

grounding: A toddler shares a brief co-viewed video call and then learns most from live play.

passage:
Snow covered Montreal and the park was closed, so Mateo put a counting song on the tablet for Rosa.
He didn't leave. He sat beside her. When the cartoon counted "uno, dos, tres", Mateo paused it and counted Rosa's toes. She giggled. He counted her socks, her spoons, her mittens drying on the heater.
Later, at dinner, Rosa held up three peas. "Tres!"
The tablet went back on the shelf. Rosa kept counting everything Mateo put in front of her.

qa.q: What did Mateo count after pausing the cartoon?
qa.a: Rosa's toes, then her socks, her spoons and her mittens.

qa.q: What do Rosa's giggles and her "Tres!" suggest she felt?
qa.a: Rosa giggled and later proudly counted three peas herself, which shows she was happy and engaged.

qa.q: Which part of Mateo's approach helped most?
qa.a: Sitting with Rosa and pausing to count real things turned the short video into a live game with him.

qa.q: What would change if Mateo had left Rosa alone with the tablet?
qa.a: Rosa might have watched the song but probably wouldn't have used "tres" at dinner, because the learning came from counting with Mateo.

grounding: A father co-views a short video with his toddler and turns it into live play.

passage:
I'm Ojas, Neelam's cousin. I stayed at her house this summer holiday.
In the afternoons, Neelam watched rhyme videos on the phone, very still, and didn't answer when I called. When it ended, she cried for more.
In the evenings, Nani sang the same rhymes live. Neelam jumped up, did the actions, and sang lines back.
I don't know what was in her head. But she looked more awake with Nani than with the phone.

qa.q: What did Neelam watch in the afternoons?
qa.a: Rhyme videos on the phone.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when the video ended?
qa.a: Neelam seemed upset and frustrated when it stopped, and cried for more.

qa.q: What could the family try in the afternoons, based on what Ojas saw?
qa.a: They could swap the phone time for live rhymes or watch together and do the actions with her, as Nani does.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when Neelam stops her to sing lines back?
qa.a: Nani is likely delighted and closer to Neelam, because they are singing together and not just side by side.

grounding: A cousin notices a toddler is passive with rhyme videos and lively with live singing.

passage:
Before Navratri, Jahnavi ate every meal with a cartoon playing on Sudha's phone. She chewed slowly and said nothing.
On the first night of the festival, Sudha left the phone in her room. She sang garba songs while feeding Jahnavi, clapping between bites. Jahnavi clapped too.
Nine days later, when Sudha sat down with the plate, Jahnavi grabbed both her hands and pushed them together. "Clap! Sing!"
Sudha sang. Jahnavi ate, bouncing.

qa.q: What did Sudha leave in her room on the first night of Navratri?
qa.a: The phone.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi grabbing Sudha's hands suggest?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels excited and eager; she now wants the singing and clapping with Sudha at mealtime. 🙂

qa.q: How could Sudha keep this going after Navratri ends?
qa.a: Sudha could keep singing or talking at meals and save any screen time for short moments they watch together.

qa.q: What is it like for Sudha when Jahnavi asks her to sing?
qa.a: Sudha probably feels closer to Jahnavi and pleased that mealtime has become a shared time again.

grounding: Over the Navratri days, a toddler moves from silent screen meals to live singing and clapping.

passage:
On a cold winter evening in their Delhi flat, Pema, two, sat watching nursery rhymes on the tablet. Her grandmother Rehana switched it off gently.
Pema whined. Rehana sat beside her with a picture book and began singing the same rhyme, clapping.
Pema watched her face, then clapped too, laughing. She pointed at the pictures.
"Again!" she said.

qa.q: What did Rehana use instead of the tablet?
qa.a: A picture book, singing the same rhyme and clapping.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when Rehana joined in?
qa.a: She felt happy and engaged, laughing and clapping.

qa.q: How can Rehana balance screens and live play?
qa.a: Keep screen time short and shared, and turn rhymes into live singing and clapping together.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel when Pema says "Again!"
qa.a: Rehana likely feels pleased and warm, seeing Pema enjoy playing with her.

grounding: Shows a toddler engaging more with live singing than a screen.

passage:
"Just put the cartoon on," said Seema's father, tired after the Christmas party.
"We'll watch it together," said her mother, Sharmila. She sat two-year-old Seema on her lap. "Look, a dog!"
"Dog!" Seema said.
"What does the dog say?"
"Woof!"
Sharmila paused it. "Can you be a dog?"
Seema crawled around the rug, barking. Her father laughed and got down on the floor to bark too.

qa.q: What did Seema say when Sharmila pointed?
qa.a: "Dog!"

qa.q: How did Seema seem to feel pretending to be a dog?
qa.a: She seemed excited and playful, crawling around the rug barking.

qa.q: How did Sharmila make screen time better?
qa.a: She watched with Seema, asked questions, and paused to play, making it live and shared.

qa.q: How is Seema's father affected by the game?
qa.a: He goes from tired to amused, laughing and joining in on the floor.

grounding: Shows a caregiver co-viewing a screen and turning it into live interaction.

passage:
Daycare note, summer term
Pradeep (2 years 6 months) has been saying fewer words than usual. His mother told us he has been watching videos for long stretches while she works from home.
Today, when Tenzin, one of our staff, sang with him and played peekaboo, he laughed and copied the words.
I shared ideas with his mother about short screen time watched together, and more talking and singing during meals. We will check in next month.

qa.q: Who sang with Pradeep today?
qa.a: Tenzin, one of our staff.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when Tenzin played peekaboo?
qa.a: He felt happy and engaged, laughing and copying words.

qa.q: What did the daycare suggest to Pradeep's mother?
qa.a: Short screen time watched together, and more talking and singing during meals.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's mother feel reading this note?
qa.a: She may feel a little worried but relieved to have practical ideas.

grounding: A daycare note on a toddler's language responding to live play more than videos.

passage:
In the village house near Anand, Aparna propped her phone on the rice tin and played a rhyme video for little Lokesh. He watched for a minute, then wandered off to pull at the broom.
His sister Kavya, seven, switched it off. "Watch, Lokesh!" She sang the same rhyme, clapping and wiggling her fingers like rain.
Lokesh sat right down in front of her. He laughed, copied the clapping, and shouted "Again!"
Aparna put the phone away and joined in.

qa.q: Where did Aparna prop her phone?
qa.a: She propped her phone on the rice tin.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when Kavya sang the rhyme?
qa.a: He felt happy and excited, laughing and copying her clapping.

qa.q: What does the scene suggest about how Aparna could use screens with Lokesh?
qa.a: She could keep screen time short and watch with him, and mostly sing and play face to face, since he joins in more when a real person is with him.

qa.q: How might Kavya feel when Lokesh shouts "Again!"?
qa.a: Kavya probably feels proud and delighted that her singing held her little brother's attention better than the phone.

grounding: Shows a toddler learning far better from live singing and play than from a video on a screen.
